traits: Black flies about 6-9 mm with a dull red thorax
Fly attached together in mating pairs
Two flights a year, roughly April-May and August-September
Splatter accumulates on car fronts and headlights

look_alikes.difference: Lovebugs have a red thorax and often fly stuck together in pairs; non-biting midges are smaller, mosquito-shaped, and don't pair up.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the body color and shape, and whether two individuals are joined together.

copy.what_it_means: Lovebugs don't bite or sting at all — they're a car-wash problem, not a pest-control problem, and no treatment prevents them since they drift in from miles around. The swarm season is short, typically about four weeks each flight.
copy.fact: Their body fluids are slightly acidic and can etch car paint if left baked on for several days — modern clear coats hold up much better than older paint.
copy.blurb: Lovebugs are a twice-a-year Florida nuisance that no treatment prevents — they drift in from miles around. The good news: they’re harmless and the swarm season is short.

tech_notes: No treatment; set expectations honestly — this is not a pest-control problem.

traits: Fuzzy, moth-like micro-fly, about 2.5-4.5 mm, resting on bathroom walls
Weak, hopping flight near sinks, tubs, and showers
Worse after a drain sits unused for a while
Larvae live in the gel-like film that builds up inside drains

look_alikes.difference: Drain flies are fuzzy and moth-shaped and stick to bathroom walls near drains; fungus gnats are slender, long-legged, and hover around houseplant soil.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the wing shape and where it was resting (drain vs. potted plant).

copy.what_it_means: The larvae live in the gel film that builds up inside drains, which is why sprays fail and a stiff brush plus an enzyme cleaner succeeds. Clean the drain film and they are usually gone within days.
copy.fact: The larvae live in the gel film inside drains — which is why sprays fail and a stiff brush plus enzyme cleaner succeeds.
copy.blurb: Clean the drain film (brush + enzyme cleaner) and they’re gone in days.

tech_notes: Non-biting, no known disease transmission. Recommend mechanical drain cleaning; treatment is rarely needed if the source is addressed.

traits: Tiny dark flies with long legs and thread-like antennae, hovering around potted plants
Weak fliers that drift rather than dart
Larvae are slender, white, and legless in the top layer of wet potting soil
Numbers track soil moisture — more gnats means soil staying too wet

look_alikes.difference: Fungus gnats are slender and long-legged and hover over houseplant soil; drain flies are fuzzy and moth-shaped and stick to bathroom walls near drains.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the wing shape and where it was resting (potted plant vs. drain).

copy.what_it_means: It's an overwatering alarm with wings — the larvae need soggy soil to survive. Let pots dry out between waterings and yellow sticky cards will catch the stragglers; most cases need no treatment at all.
copy.fact: It's an overwatering alarm with wings — the larvae need soggy soil to survive.
copy.blurb: Let pots dry between waterings; yellow sticky cards catch the stragglers.

tech_notes: Harmless nuisance tied to overwatering; advise cultural fix (drying cycle) before any treatment.
